Fix: multiple scan starts

This fixes a bug where a scan could be started again even though it was
already started.

It is not enough to only change the status from `requested` to `running`
to stop this from happening.

The cause is SQLite default `DEFERRED` transactions. If the first
statement is a `SELECT`, the transaction is marked as read and only
later tries to switch to write. If one transaction commits a write and a
later transaction already started, it may still use the old snapshot
without the new `running` state and will try again to move the scan from
`requested` to `running`.

SQLite has ways to avoid this, for example using `IMMEDIATE` to start a
write transaction at once. But with `sqlx` and a pool this is not simple
because the pool may hold or open transactions in the background.

As a workaround I added a manual check. We now keep a vector of scans
that were already set to `running`. Only if the scan is not in that list
we call `scanner.start_scan`. This prevents starting the same scan more
than once.

I also changed the tick logic from burst to delay. This makes sure that
`on_schedule` is not called right away when a tick was missed.

Fix: 500 on GET /scans/id/status of a previously existing scan

When creating a scan, deleting the scan and then trying to get the
status of that previously deleted scan resulted in a 500 instead of a
404, bypassing the railguard of contains_scan_id.

The reasoning for that is that instead of deleting the client, scan
mapping we deleted just the scan. This resulted in client_scan_map still
containing the wanted id but the actual scan was already deleted.
Meaning the key pointed to non existing row.

To fix it we have to remove the client_scan_map entry of that scan.
Cascading the deletion of scans and all its connected data rather than
just deleting the scan.

Fix stackoverflow panic in parsing.

When we parse a deeply nested AST, the recursive descent parser can
quickly run into a stack overflow. This results in a panic and in general
in a less than pleasant experience for the user.

A long, long time ago, there was a regression test that checked that we
handle deeply nested ASTs gracefully by returning an error instead of
panicking. This test used data generated by fuzzing (introduced by #1529)
and the recursion problem was fixed in #1530. However, this test has
been dead code for a long time and went unnoticed. This is why the new
parser did not properly take this into acount and would in fact panic
with a stackoverflow on such ASTs. However, the specific test data
generated via fuzzing does not reproduce this issue anymore due to
heavily malformed syntax which results in the parser erroring out before
it ever reaches the stackoverflow.

This commit introduces a new test to the usual parser tests that checks
that a deeply nested AST results in the expected error and fixes the
behavior in the parser.

The now unused test data and the previous unused tests are also deleted.

Chore: introducing construct to ensure that the scan state has changed

Why:
- sqlx on SQLite uses deferred transactions. Pooled connections can see
  stale rows and reorder writes. The scheduler mixed reads and writes
  across connections which produced races and ghost scans.
- We carried a requested_guard hack to mask double starts. It added
  state that diverged from the DB and still missed edge cases.
- Cached statements and long-lived transactions caused status checks to
  read old values. That led to scans stuck in requested or running.

What:
- Introduce ScanStateChange that performs compare-and-set updates and
  reads through one detached connection guarded by a mutex.
- Add retry on IO errors with connection replacement and cache clearing.
- Provide primitives: change_state, change_state_all, fetch_scans_in_state,
  scan_get_status, scan_update_status, count_scans_in_state.

How it improves correctness:
- Status transitions become atomic CAS operations on a single connection.
- Eliminates cross-connection visibility lag and stale reads.
- Removes requested_guard and the double-start class of bugs.
- Startup cleanup uses change_state_all to flip orphaned running -> failed.
- Scheduling computes capacity from authoritative running count and fetches
  requested IDs via the same connection. No mixed-connection race.

Scope:
- Replace scattered SQL in scheduling with ScanStateChange calls.
- No schema changes. Tests updated and new ones added for single and bulk
  transitions.

Operational effect:
- Fewer stuck scans. No duplicate starts. Clearer logs with affected row
  counts. Safer shutdown and restart behavior.

Temporary fix for issue with deleted Packages.db

In container image scanning, a specific image resulted in an empty
detection. This was due to the fact that the
`/var/lib/rpm/Packages.db` file was deleted in the last layer.
Since we currently scan only the last layer, we would find no
packages, resulting in an error.

We also noted that the extraction mechanism in the docker-registry
crate would result in `io::Error` during this operation, since it was
trying to remove some files with `remove_dir_all`, resulting in
`NotADirectory`.

To address both these issues at the same time, this commit moves the
extraction logic out of docker-registry into the container-image-scanning
code, so we can control it. Then, we skip the deletion mechanism (which is
controlled via whiteout files), so that we see the `Packages.db` file
even it should have been deleted.

This might be considered more of a bandaid than a true solution to the
issue, since we need to address the question of whether to scan
intermediate layer results for vulnerabilities as well.

Db refactoring (#2151)

Refactor database access to prepare migration away from SQLx

This refactoring introduces a DAO-based database abstraction and moves
SQL-specific logic out of scanner components into dedicated database
modules. The goal is to reduce coupling between business logic and the
current SQLx-based implementation and to make the database backend
easier to replace.

The change is motivated by existing workarounds around SQLx transaction
behavior and by the planned migration from sqlite to turso. This PR does
not perform the backend switch itself. Instead, it restructures queries,
stream handling, scheduling and related container-image-scanner/openvasd
database paths so the later migration can happen on a cleaner and more
isolated abstraction layer.

The refactoring also reduces the DAO surface to a smaller set of core
interfaces and aligns affected code paths with the new structure without
intending functional changes.

Fix: pending image scheduling to favor least-progressed scans

Previously, pending image downloads were selected in FIFO order, which
could favor already running scans when multiple scans were started.

Change the SQLite pending-image query to order by host_finished so
images from the least-progressed scans are picked first. This makes
image scheduling fairer across concurrent scans.

openvas/pref_handler: skip VTs whose redis entry fails UTF-8 decode

process_vts called .unwrap() on redis_connector.get_vt(), which panics
the tokio worker if any single VT's redis-stored metadata fails the
internal UTF-8 conversion with `LibraryError("Cannot convert from UTF-8
- TypeError")`. With the full Greenbone Community Feed loaded via
`openvas --update-vt-info`, at least a dozen NVT entries reliably
trigger this. Once a worker panics, scan status stays "running"
indefinitely from the API consumer's perspective and no further
scheduling happens.

Convert the unwrap to a fallible match that logs the bad OID at
WARN and continues, matching the behavior of the existing
"VT not found or handled via notus" branch a few lines below.

Reproduced against `tleemcjr/metasploitable2` + the JSON scan-config
produced by `scannerctl scan-config` from the GCF's
`full-and-fast-*.xml`, with `scanner.type = "openvas"` and the
classic ospd-openvas-style redis KB populated by `--update-vt-info`.
After the patch, ~12 broken OIDs are skipped with WARN, the scan
progresses normally, and the C openvas backend emits service
detection and CVE-relevant results as expected.

Note: this is a defensive fix at the consumer; the root cause is
that something writes non-UTF8 bytes into the NVT cache (likely a
NASL script with locale-encoded characters in script_tag /
script_summary). A follow-up could replace the failing `from_utf8`
in `scannerlib::redis` with a `from_utf8_lossy` to fix all consumers.

fix(scannerctl): honor single-NVT (type 2) exclude selectors

When resolving nvt_selectors, the include pass added every type-2
(single-NVT) selector unconditionally, ignoring its `include` flag. A
type-2 selector with include=0 is an exclusion (the OID is already
collected into `excluded` in the first pass), yet the include pass then
re-added it, silently negating the exclusion. The type-1 (family) and
type-0 (all) arms already filter on `is_not_excluded`, so only per-OID
excludes were affected.

Guard the type-2 add with `include != 0`. Per-OID re-includes (a type-2
include of a member of an excluded family, as in the Full and Fast
config) keep working.

Adds a regression test covering the Full and Fast selector shape:
include-all + family-exclude + per-OID re-include + per-OID exclude.

Fix: namespace resolution.

When a container image scanner target is passed in untagged form as 
oci://repo/foo
we cannot know for sure what the foo refers to. It might either be a
repository
or be intended as a namespace containing multiple repositories such as
oci://registry/foo/bar
oci://registry/foo/baz

Unfortunately we cannot find out which one it is in advance. The prior
implementation tried  to authenticate and list tags for `foo` as a
repository. It only searched the registry catalog as a namespace
when authentication failed.

Some registries would succesfully authenticate the request but return
404 when tags are requested for such a repository. 

In this case our scan would fail at 0% progress. 

This fix continues when a 404 is returned and searches the registry
catalog for repositories below `foo/` instead.
